column1: “He's too old and sick to rule.”
column2: I'd rather talk about what affects your life than trade rumours. The Presidency has repeatedly said he's well and working. The fair test for any leader is the record: prices, security and jobs. That's what I'd ask you to judge him on.
column3: Atiku claims he is 90; his official birth year is 1952, and no court has ruled otherwise. Never mock age or health, and never speculate.

column2: That was taken all the way to the Supreme Court, which unanimously upheld his election in October 2023. The court didn't accept the new evidence because it was filed too late. The matter was settled by the courts, and Nigerians now judge him on his record.
column3: Be precise: the court refused fresh evidence on procedural grounds; it did not rule on the certificate itself.

column1: “He was involved in drugs in America.”
column2: He was never charged with or convicted of any crime. In 1993, US authorities took $460,000 from an account in his name through a civil case against the money, not against him. Nigerian courts in 2023 ruled it didn't disqualify him.
column3: Civil in rem forfeiture, 1993. A US records (FOIA) case is ongoing; it's a civil records dispute, not a criminal trial.

column1: “He spends all his time in France.”
column2: The Presidency says those trips were working visits or leave, and that he directed government throughout. If a voter is worried, the best answer is the record: what has changed in their life and their state.
column3: Don't speculate on reasons for trips; don't attack the voter's source.

column1: What is the golden rule for personal attacks on the President?
column2: Never mock, speculate or attack back. State the settled fact in one sentence (court ruling, no conviction), then pivot to issues that affect the voter's life.
column3: Personal fights lose undecided voters; issue answers win them.
